Leonard Thompson, J. Christian Wilson and many historians argue there is no reliable evidence of a general Domitianic persecution: Dio does not mention Christians, the Christian identification comes later, 1 Clement's phrase is vague and its date is debated (Robinson argued for about 70), and Revelation names only one martyr, Antipas (2:13). By contrast Nero's massacre of Christians at Rome after the fire of 64 is firmly attested (Tacitus, Annals 15.44), so if the book reflects a power drunk with 'the blood of the saints' (17:6), the Neronian setting is the one clearly documented. Thompson himself still dates the book under Domitian on other grounds, which shows that this point alone does not settle the date.
The Nicolaitans as an established sect

The Nicolaitans appear at Ephesus and Pergamum as a recognised party with a known teaching (2:6, 15), associated with eating food sacrificed to idols and sexual immorality (2:14-15, 20). Irenaeus links them to Nicolas of Antioch, one of the seven chosen in Acts 6:5 (Against Heresies 1.26.3). Late-date advocates argue that a named sect with a settled doctrine implies time to develop, and that its absence from Paul's letters to Ephesus and Colossae suggests it arose after Paul.

The issues are exactly those Paul faced at Corinth in the mid-50s (1 Corinthians 6:12-20; 8-10), so the teaching need not be late. If Irenaeus is right that the group traces back to Nicolas, its founder was active from the 30s, giving it ample time to spread by the 60s. Paul's letters do not catalogue every faction, and the Ephesian elders had already been warned of false teachers arising among them (Acts 20:29-30).
Irenaeus reconsidered: was it John, not the vision, who was 'seen'?

Early-date advocates argue that Irenaeus' testimony is weaker than it looks. The Greek verb heōrathē ('was seen') has no stated subject; the nearest antecedent is 'him who saw the apocalypse', so Irenaeus' point may be that John himself was seen, alive and accessible, almost in Irenaeus' own generation, and could have told the Antichrist's name had it been needed. Irenaeus elsewhere says John remained with the elders of Asia until Trajan's time (2.22.5; 3.3.4), which fits that sense. He also makes chronological errors elsewhere, and in the same chapter he admits that copies with 616 were circulating, showing that he did not have complete information about the book's early history.

Most commentators judge the vision to be the natural subject: Irenaeus is arguing about when the apocalypse was seen, the old Latin translation renders 'it was seen' (visum est), and the phrase 'not long ago, almost in our own generation' suits dating an event rather than describing a long life. Eusebius, who read Irenaeus in full, understood him to date the vision, and no ancient writer took the sentence the other way. An error elsewhere in Irenaeus does not show an error here, on a matter of recent Asian church memory transmitted through Polycarp.
Tertullian: John plunged into boiling oil at Rome, then exiled

Tertullian, praising the church at Rome, says it was there that 'Peter endured a passion like his Lord's, where Paul was crowned with a death like John's [the Baptist], where the apostle John was first plunged, unhurt, into boiling oil, and thence sent to his island exile.' The grouping with Peter and Paul, both martyred under Nero, suggests a Neronian setting for John's ordeal and exile. Jerome, reporting Tertullian, says it was Nero who had John thrown into the oil (Against Jovinian 1.26). If the island exile followed directly, it too falls under Nero.

Tertullian names no emperor, and the sentence lists Rome's apostolic glories rather than giving a chronology. Elsewhere he calls Domitian 'a portion of Nero in cruelty' who began a persecution but soon stopped and recalled those he had banished (Apology 5), which fits a Domitianic exile. Jerome, who attributes the oil to Nero, himself dates the Patmos exile and the writing of Revelation to Domitian's fourteenth year (On Illustrious Men 9), so he evidently did not treat the two events as simultaneous.
Muratorian fragment: Paul followed John's example in writing to seven churches

The Muratorian fragment, a list of New Testament books traditionally dated to the late second century, says that 'the blessed apostle Paul himself, following the order of his predecessor John, writes by name to only seven churches', and later that John too, 'though he writes to seven churches in the Apocalypse, nevertheless speaks to all.' Early-date advocates argue that if Paul followed John's pattern, John's letters to the seven churches came before Paul's letters were complete, which places Revelation before Paul's death in the mid-60s, at least in the fragment author's understanding.

Read literally, the fragment would put Revelation before all Paul's letters, around 50 or earlier, which no one accepts; it is better read as a theological comparison in which John is Paul's 'predecessor' in apostolic standing and the number seven signifies the whole church. The fragment's Latin is notoriously corrupt, and its date is itself disputed, with some scholars placing it in the fourth century. It shows no awareness of when or under whom Revelation was written.
Epiphanius: John prophesied in the time of Claudius

Epiphanius of Salamis, about 375, twice says that John prophesied on the island of Patmos in the time of Claudius Caesar (Panarion 51.12; 51.33). Claudius died in 54, which is too early even for most early-date advocates, but they note that Nero's official name was Nero Claudius Caesar, so Epiphanius may preserve a tradition placing the exile under Nero. At the least, his statement shows that the Domitianic date was not universal in the fourth century.

Epiphanius is late and notoriously careless with chronology, and a date under Claudius conflicts with every other datum, including the early-date case itself. Reading 'Claudius' as a reference to Nero is a conjecture made to rescue the statement. A single idiosyncratic remark three centuries after the event cannot outweigh Irenaeus.
The Syriac heading: 'banished by Nero Caesar'

In the Syriac translation of Revelation made in the sixth century, the book carries a heading describing it as the revelation given to John the evangelist on the island of Patmos, 'into which he was thrown by Nero Caesar.' Early-date advocates cite this as evidence that at least one stream of eastern tradition remembered the exile as Neronian, independent of Irenaeus and Eusebius.

The heading is a scribal title from the sixth century or later, roughly five centuries after the event, and Revelation was not part of the original Syriac canon, so it cannot carry an early Syrian tradition about the book. It may reflect the identification of the beast with Nero or simple confusion among persecuting emperors. Manuscript titles are widely recognised as secondary and are rarely given weight in dating.
Arethas: Jerusalem's destruction 'not yet' inflicted

Arethas of Caesarea in Cappadocia, writing in the early tenth century, applies parts of the sixth seal and the sealing of the 144,000 (6:12-17; 7:1-8) to the Jewish War, and remarks that when John received these oracles the destruction of the Jews by the Romans had not yet happened. Early-date advocates cite this as evidence that a pre-70 reading of Revelation survived within the Greek commentary tradition.

Arethas wrote some eight centuries after the event, and his remark is an inference from his own interpretation of the seals rather than an independent historical report. He worked within a Greek commentary tradition, building on Andrew of Caesarea, that also knew Eusebius' Domitianic account. An exegetical opinion about what certain visions refer to is not evidence of when the book was written.
The temple and altar measured: the temple still stands (11:1-2)

John is told to 'measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple... for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months' (11:1-2). Early-date advocates read this as the Jerusalem temple still standing, and the forty-two months as roughly the Roman campaign from spring 67 to August 70, echoing Jesus' word that Jerusalem would be 'trampled by the Gentiles' (Luke 21:24). The same chapter places 'the great city' where 'their Lord was crucified' (11:8). Had the temple lain in ruins for twenty-five years, a command to measure it and a prophecy of the city's trampling would be strange.

The scene is visionary and modelled on Ezekiel 40-48 and Zechariah 2:1-5, where a temple and city are measured that did not then physically exist (Ezekiel wrote after the first temple was destroyed), so measuring no more requires a standing building now than it did then. Most late-date commentators (Beale, Bauckham, Koester) read the temple as the worshipping people of God, protected inwardly while exposed outwardly, an image the New Testament uses elsewhere (1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Peter 2:5). And if 11:1-2 were a literal forecast written before 70, it would promise the sanctuary's preservation while only the outer court was trampled, whereas in fact the sanctuary itself was burned.
The seven kings: 'five have fallen, one is' (17:9-11)

The seven heads are seven hills and seven kings: 'five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he comes he must remain only a little while' (17:9-10). Roman and Jewish writers often counted the Caesars from Julius (Suetonius' Lives of the Caesars; 4 Ezra 12:14-15 makes Augustus the second), so the five fallen are Julius, Augustus, Tiberius, Gaius and Claudius, the one who 'is' is Nero, and the short-lived seventh is Galba (June 68 to January 69). Counting from Augustus makes Galba the one who 'is', still before 70. The classicist Albert Bell argued that no natural count makes Domitian the sixth, and that late-date attempts 'make nonsense of the seer's list'.

There are many possible starting points (Julius, Augustus, Caligula as first persecutor, or Nero) and many possible rules (whether to include Galba, Otho and Vitellius, who reigned only months in the civil war, or only emperors deified by the senate), and some counts reach Vespasian or Domitian. Many late-date commentators (Beale, Bauckham) take seven as a symbol of the whole succession of Roman power, with 'one is' marking the present late in that sequence and the 'eighth who belongs to the seven' a Nero-like return; Aune suggests the list may come from an earlier stage of composition under Vespasian, kept in the final edition. The passage itself says 'this calls for a mind with wisdom' (17:9), a hint that a simple head count may not be intended.
666 and 616: the number of Nero Caesar

'Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666' (13:18). The Greek Neron Kaisar written in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr) adds up to 666 (50+200+6+50+100+60+200), and this spelling is attested in an Aramaic document from Wadi Murabba'at dated by 'Nero Caesar' (Hillers 1963). Strikingly, some early copies, including those Irenaeus knew and the papyrus P115 (Oxyrhynchus 4499), read 616, exactly the value of the Latin form Nero Caesar (nrw qsr) without the final n, as if scribes knew the Nero solution. If the beast is the reigning emperor who persecuted Christians, the book fits naturally under Nero.

Many late-date scholars also accept the Nero gematria (Bauckham, Aune, Koester) but read it within the expectation of a returning Nero, so a reference to Nero does not by itself date the book to his reign. Irenaeus, who discussed the number at length within a century, did not think of Nero, and the solution requires spelling a Greek name in Hebrew letters for Greek-speaking readers. Others read 666 symbolically, as humanity falling persistently short of seven, or note that it is a triangular number, so the identification, though attractive, is not certain.
'What must soon take place' and 'the time is near'

The book opens and closes with time indicators: it shows 'the things that must soon take place' (1:1; 22:6), declares 'the time is near' (1:3; 22:10), and John is told not to seal up the prophecy (22:10), reversing Daniel's command to seal his book 'until the time of the end' (Daniel 12:4). Early-date advocates argue that these expressions point to events within the first readers' lifetimes, and that the greatest such events within reach were the Neronian persecution, the Jewish War and the fall of Jerusalem (66-70).

Even if the language means near in time, it does not fix the date: a book written under Domitian could equally promise imminent trial for the churches (2:10; 3:10) and imminent judgment on Rome. Many interpreters read 'soon' within the New Testament conviction that the last days have already begun (Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18), or as stressing certainty and suddenness, God's timing not being ours (2 Peter 3:8). Whatever 'soon' means, it cannot by itself decide between 65 and 95.
'Those who pierced him' and the tribes of the land (1:7)

'Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth (or land) will wail on account of him' (1:7). The verse draws on Zechariah 12:10-14, where the mourning tribes are the clans of Israel, and early-date advocates argue that 'those who pierced him' were the first-century generation. The book's theme verse would then announce a coming in judgment on the land of Israel within that generation, as in Jesus' words about the Son of Man coming on the clouds before 'this generation' passed (Matthew 24:30, 34), which requires a date before 70.

The verse combines Daniel 7:13 with Zechariah 12:10 and widens Zechariah's mourning clans into 'all the tribes of the earth', echoing the promise to bless 'all the families of the earth' (Genesis 12:3; 28:14), while 'every eye will see him' is universal. Most commentators therefore see Christ's final coming, with 'those who pierced him' representing all who reject him (compare John 19:37). Even if it is read as judgment on Israel, the verse announces a theme; it does not date the writing.
No mention of Jerusalem's destruction

J. A. T. Robinson's central argument for redating the New Testament was that no book refers to the fall of Jerusalem and its temple in 70 as a past event, though it was the most traumatic event of the century for Judaism and for Jewish Christianity. Revelation is full of temple imagery, judgment on 'the great city' and reflection on Israel (7:4-8; 11:1-13; 21:12), yet it never says that the temple has fallen. For a book so concerned with God's judgments, early-date advocates argue, silence about the greatest judgment of the era is best explained if it had not yet happened.

Arguments from silence are weak, especially for a book written to mainly Gentile churches in Asia whose pressing issues were Rome, local synagogues and civic idolatry. Revelation narrates no past historical events in detail at all, and other writings commonly dated after 70, such as the Gospel of John, do not mention the destruction explicitly either (though Robinson dated those early too). Late-date commentators also see a destroyed temple presupposed in the visionary temple of chapter 11 and in the new Jerusalem that has no temple (21:22).
The sealing of Israel's tribes before the winds of judgment (7:1-8)

Before the four winds of judgment are released on 'the land', 144,000 servants of God from the twelve tribes of Israel are sealed for protection (7:1-8). Early-date advocates read this as the preservation of Jewish Christians before Jerusalem's fall, comparing the tradition that the Jerusalem church fled to Pella before the siege after an oracle (Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3) and Jesus' command to flee to the mountains (Luke 21:20-21). Such a protective sealing makes most sense, they argue, while that judgment still lay ahead.

Most commentators see the 144,000 as a symbolic portrait of the whole people of God, organised as an army of Israel, since John immediately 'looks' and sees a countless multitude from every nation (7:9), the same pattern by which he 'hears' of a Lion and sees a Lamb (5:5-6). The tribal list is irregular (Dan is omitted, Judah comes first), suggesting a theological rather than ethnic census. The Pella tradition is itself debated by historians, and in any case a symbol of protection through tribulation fits any date.
Rough Greek: written before John's Gospel

Revelation's Greek is rough, full of Semitic constructions and grammatical irregularities, while John's Gospel is written in simple but correct Greek; Dionysius of Alexandria already noticed the difference in the third century (Eusebius, Church History 7.25). B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, assuming the same author, argued that the Apocalypse must be the earlier work, written before John had lived long in a Greek-speaking setting, with the Gospel following a generation later. On that reasoning a book in John's less polished Greek belongs in the 60s.

Most scholars now think the irregularities are deliberate, an elevated style imitating Hebrew prophecy, since John elsewhere uses correctly the very constructions he breaks (Charles, Beale). Many doubt that the same author wrote both books (Dionysius himself concluded they were different authors), or allow for a secretary in the Gospel, and the Gospel's own date is uncertain. Style cannot place a book within a particular decade.

Most partial preterists need the early date. Their reading takes much of chapters 4-19 as prophecy of the Jewish War, the fall of Jerusalem and the temple, and the Neronian persecution, which cannot be prophecy if the book was written in 95. This is why Kenneth Gentry and others have devoted whole books to the date. A minority of preterist-leaning interpreters accept a late date and apply the book's judgments to pagan Rome instead, with its fall in the fifth century or its earlier humbling, but that is a different reading from the Jerusalem-centred preterism usually meant.

Full preterism requires the early date. It holds that every prophecy in Revelation, including Christ's coming, the resurrection and the new heavens and earth, was fulfilled by AD 70; if Revelation was written in 95 it would be prophesying events already past. Writers such as J. Stuart Russell and Max King therefore defend the early date as essential.

Historicism does not depend on the date in the same way, because it reads Revelation as a sweep of church history from John's day to the end. Classic historicists generally accepted the Domitianic date and began the sequence of seals in the late first or second century (E. B. Elliott began the first seal around the death of Domitian), but an earlier date would only move the starting point back a generation.

Futurism is compatible with either date, since it places the main events of chapters 4-22 at the end of the age. Most futurists (John Walvoord, Robert Thomas) hold the late date, and many see it as ruling out the preterist alternative; but a futurist could accept an early date and still read the seals, trumpets and bowls as future.

Idealism is largely indifferent to the date, because it reads the book as portraying timeless conflict between Christ and evil rather than forecasting particular events. Most idealist and modified idealist commentators (William Hendriksen, G. K. Beale) assume the late date and set the book against Domitian's Asia, but the method works equally well with Nero's Rome as the first expression of the pattern.

Amillennialism rests on its reading of Revelation 20 and the structure of recapitulation, not on the date. Most amillennial commentators hold the late date (Hendriksen, Beale, Kim Riddlebarger), but some, such as Jay Adams in The Time Is at Hand, combined amillennialism with an early date and a largely preterist reading of the earlier chapters.

Many contemporary postmillennialists (Kenneth Gentry, David Chilton, Keith Mathison, Gary DeMar) combine their view with partial preterism and so need the early date for their reading of Revelation's judgments as fulfilled in AD 70. Postmillennialism as such rests on broader biblical themes of the gospel's worldwide success, and older postmillennialists did not tie it to an early Revelation.

The spiritual understanding reads Revelation as the unveiling of Jesus Christ and his finished work, a present reality rather than a calendar, so for most of its teachers the date matters little. Some within this stream, who describe the passing of the old covenant order as completed in AD 70, find the early date congenial, but the core reading of the Lamb at the centre of the throne does not depend on it.

Most modern scholars, across critical and evangelical lines, favour a date under Domitian, around 95, chiefly because of Irenaeus' early and specific testimony, supported by Victorinus, Eusebius and Jerome, and because several internal features (the condition of the churches, 'Babylon' for Rome, the Nero legend, the imperial cult in Asia) fit the Flavian period comfortably. A significant and learned minority, from Westcott, Hort and Lightfoot to Robinson and Gentry, holds that the internal evidence of the standing temple, the sixth king and the number of Nero's name points to the late 60s, and that the external tradition largely depends on one ambiguous sentence. Neither side's arguments are decisive: the strongest late-date evidence is external and the strongest early-date evidence is internal, and each has a credible reply. Some scholars, notably Aune, propose a book that grew over time, which would let both sets of evidence be partly right. Readers should hold their conclusion with humility, and should note that only some views (especially partial and full preterism) depend on the answer, while futurism, idealism, historicism and the millennial positions can stand with either date.

In AD 66 Judea rose against Rome, and four years later Jerusalem and its temple lay in ruins. Almost everything we know about those years comes from one man, Flavius Josephus, who fought on the Jewish side, changed sides, and watched the end from the Roman lines. This retelling follows his Jewish War scene by scene, with his own words in William Whiston's 1737 translation and a map of the city that changes as the siege tightens. Along the way it notes where Christian readers have seen Jesus' warnings about Jerusalem fulfilled, and where historians urge caution about Josephus himself.

Joseph son of Matthias was born in Jerusalem in AD 37 or 38 into a priestly family, and as a young man went to Rome on an embassy to Nero's court. When the revolt broke out in 66, the provisional government in Jerusalem made him commander in Galilee, where he fortified towns and quarrelled bitterly with rivals such as John of Gischala. In 67 Vespasian besieged him in the hill town of Jotapata for forty-seven days; when it fell, Josephus hid in a cave with forty others, survived a suicide pact, and surrendered. Brought before Vespasian, he announced that the general and his son Titus would become emperors, and when Vespasian was proclaimed in 69 he freed his prisoner, who took the family name Flavius. Josephus spent the siege of Jerusalem at Titus' side as an interpreter, calling on the defenders to surrender while his own parents were inside the walls. Afterwards he lived in Rome on an imperial pension, in a house once owned by Vespasian, and wrote the Jewish War in Greek around AD 75 to 79, having first composed a version in Aramaic for readers in the East. He later wrote the Antiquities of the Jews, an autobiography (the Life) and a defence of Judaism (Against Apion), and died around the end of the first century.
Written under Flavian patronage

Josephus wrote in Rome as a client of Vespasian and Titus, and says he presented the work to them for approval. He consistently portrays Titus as merciful and insists the temple burned against his wishes, yet the later Christian writer Sulpicius Severus, possibly drawing on a lost section of Tacitus, says Titus' council decided to destroy it. Most historians think Josephus' picture of a reluctant Titus is at least partly apologetic.
Speeches and set pieces

Like other Greek and Roman historians, Josephus composed the speeches he puts in his characters' mouths, including his own appeals at the walls and Eleazar's long address at Masada, where no surviving witness could have recorded it. They tell us what Josephus thought fitting to say, not a transcript. Scenes such as Mary's cannibalism also echo the curses of Deuteronomy 28 and the siege stories of the Bible, so literary shaping is likely even where the core event is real.
Ancient numbers

Figures such as 1,100,000 dead or 2,700,200 Passover pilgrims are almost certainly too high for a city whose population most scholars estimate in the tens of thousands, swollen by refugees and pilgrims to perhaps a few hundred thousand. Tacitus gives a lower figure of 600,000 besieged. The numbers convey the scale of the catastrophe as Josephus saw it rather than a census.
A survivor justifying himself

Josephus had to explain why a Jewish general was alive and comfortable in Rome. He blames the war on a small band of 'robbers' and 'tyrants', on bad Roman governors and on God's judgment, while presenting the priestly aristocracy he belonged to as reluctant moderates. His own conduct at Jotapata is told in a way that makes his surrender look like obedience to God, and his autobiography contradicts the War on several details of his Galilean command.
Reliable where he can be checked

For all this, Josephus was an eyewitness with access to Roman commentaries, and where archaeology can test him he often holds up. The Burnt House in the Jewish Quarter, excavated by Nahman Avigad, preserved a home of the priestly Kathros family destroyed by fire in 70, with a spear and the arm bones of a young woman. Along the western wall of the Temple Mount, huge Herodian stones thrown down by the Romans still lie where they crashed onto the paved street below. His descriptions of Jerusalem's walls, Masada's ramp and palaces also broadly match what excavators have found.
Spring AD 66 (Artemisius)
Florus raids the temple treasury
The temple and the upper market, Jerusalem

Judea had been simmering for years under a run of greedy Roman procurators, and Gessius Florus was the worst of them in Josephus' telling. In the spring of 66, with trouble already flaring in Caesarea, Florus sent men to take seventeen talents from the sacred treasury, claiming the emperor needed it. Crowds poured into the temple courts shouting for Caesar to free them from Florus, and some wits carried a basket round begging small change for the 'poor' governor. Florus answered with soldiers. He marched on Jerusalem, demanded the mockers be handed over, and when the leading men could not produce them he let his troops loose on the upper market. Josephus says about 3,600 people died that day, including Jews of equestrian rank who were scourged and crucified. Queen Berenice, who was in the city, pleaded barefoot before Florus' tribunal and was ignored.

…but Florus acted herein as if he had been hired, and blew up the war into a flame, and sent some to take seventeen talents out of the sacred treasure, and pretended that Caesar wanted them. At this the people were in confusion immediately, and ran together to the temple, with prodigious clamors, and called upon Caesar by name, and besought him to free them from the tyranny of Florus.
Jewish War 2.14.6
Summer AD 66
The sacrifice for Caesar is stopped
The temple, Jerusalem

For decades the priests had offered a daily sacrifice on behalf of the emperor and the Roman people, a token of loyalty that let Judea keep its own worship. In the summer of 66 Eleazar son of Ananias, the young captain of the temple and son of a former high priest, persuaded the officiating priests to accept no more gifts or sacrifices from foreigners. Senior priests and leading Pharisees argued against it, warning that it amounted to a declaration of war, but they were overruled. Josephus calls this the true beginning of the war. Fighting broke out between the peace party in the upper city and the rebels holding the temple; the rebels burned the public archives with their records of debts, took the fortress of Antonia, and besieged the Roman garrison in Herod's palace. The garrison surrendered on a promise of safe conduct and was massacred once it had laid down its arms. About the same time rebels seized the desert fortress of Masada.

At the same time Eleazar, the son of Ananias the high priest, a very bold youth, who was at that time governor of the temple, persuaded those that officiated in the Divine service to receive no gift or sacrifice for any foreigner. And this was the true beginning of our war with the Romans; for they rejected the sacrifice of Caesar on this account…
Jewish War 2.17.2
Autumn AD 66 (Hyperberetaeus)
Cestius Gallus besieges, then withdraws
Mount Scopus, Bezetha and the Beth-horon pass

Cestius Gallus, the governor of Syria, marched south with the Twelfth Legion and thousands of auxiliaries and allied troops. He camped on Mount Scopus, burned the new northern suburb of Bezetha, and pressed his attack to the north wall of the temple itself, his men locking shields over their heads to undermine it. Josephus believed the city was on the point of falling, and that some leading citizens were ready to open the gates. Then, for reasons Josephus could not explain, Cestius called off the assault and began to retreat. The rebels harried his column all the way down the pass of Beth-horon, and the Romans lost thousands of men, their siege engines and their baggage. The victory convinced many waverers that God was with the revolt. Christian tradition, recorded by Eusebius in the fourth century and not by Josephus, adds that the Jerusalem church left the city before the war, warned by an oracle, and settled at Pella beyond the Jordan; many Christian readers have connected that flight with Jesus' instruction to flee when they saw Jerusalem surrounded by armies.
